title: A city before the familiar empires
hook: Long before the Inca, people were building on a grand scale.
story: In the Supe Valley, communities built monumental platforms and sunken courts. Caral formed part of a network of settlements with complex shared ceremonial life.
consequence: People organised labour and resources to create a lasting urban landscape.
caution: This is an approximate anchor within a site history spanning roughly 3000–1800 BCE. A large monument does not tell us exactly how its builders experienced their society.

title: Making power outlast a lifetime
hook: How do people turn belief into a mountain of stone?
story: Egypt’s pyramid fields grew through the work of skilled builders and large systems of organisation. Royal burial monuments expressed religious beliefs and the reach of state power.
consequence: Architecture made political and religious authority visible across generations.
caution: This approximate date represents the Old Kingdom pyramid landscape, not a precise completion date for every monument.

title: An African kingdom in stone
hook: Towering monuments preserve the outline of a powerful world.
story: Aksum was the centre of a major kingdom in the Ethiopian highlands. Its stelae, tombs, and palace remains reveal a society with wealth, skilled craftspeople, and far-reaching influence.
consequence: Monuments preserved traces of a major African political centre.
caution: The kingdom lasted for centuries. This approximate anchor does not date all its monuments or reduce its history to one ruler.

title: Power on the high plateau
hook: A city nearly four kilometres above the sea shapes a wider world.
story: Near Lake Titicaca, Tiwanaku became a major spiritual and political centre. Its monumental buildings reflect an influential Andean society distinct from the later Inca world.
consequence: A highland centre projected influence across a much wider region.
caution: The date sits within its period of major influence, approximately 500–900 CE. The exact nature of its political control is debated.

title: A story you can walk through
hook: What if a building could guide your thoughts?
story: Builders in Java created a vast Buddhist monument around a hill. Terraces, carved reliefs, and stupas turned ideas about spiritual life into a place people could move through.
consequence: Architecture became a powerful medium for sharing belief.
caution: Construction belongs broadly to the eighth and ninth centuries. The monument expresses a particular Buddhist tradition, not all beliefs across Asia.

title: The city that worked with water
hook: Beyond the temples lies a world of reservoirs and canals.
story: Successive Khmer capitals formed a vast landscape of temples, roads, settlements, and water structures. Engineering and belief were woven into the life of the city.
consequence: Shared infrastructure helped sustain a large and complex urban world.
caution: Angkor developed between the ninth and fifteenth centuries. This date is a viewing point in that long history, not the construction date of Angkor Wat.

title: A sacred world carved downward
hook: Instead of stacking stones, builders remove the mountain.
story: At Lalibela, churches were carved into rock and connected by passages and trenches. The complex became an important place of Ethiopian Christian pilgrimage.
consequence: A religious vision became an extraordinary built landscape.
caution: The churches’ chronology is not fully settled. Their creation is traditionally associated with King Lalibela around the twelfth and thirteenth centuries.

title: An ocean at the doorstep
hook: A Swahili port brings faraway worlds to the same shore.
story: Kilwa prospered through Indian Ocean trade. Its merchants exchanged goods from the African interior alongside ceramics and other objects from distant parts of Asia.
consequence: Coastal communities helped connect inland Africa with ocean-spanning networks.
caution: This approximate anchor marks a period of prosperity, not the beginning of the settlement. Trade also involved unequal power and human exploitation.

sources.title: UNESCO · Kilwa Kisiwani and Songo Mnara

title: Metal letters before Gutenberg
hook: An old book changes the usual story of invention.
story: The Buddhist text Jikji was printed with movable metal type at Heungdeok Temple. Its surviving second volume is evidence of Korean metal-type printing before Gutenberg’s Bible.
consequence: A surviving object reveals a broader geography of technological innovation.
caution: This does not prove that Gutenberg copied Korean methods. Similar technologies can have different histories of development and use.

sources.title: UNESCO · Jikji, Memory of the World

title: A city shaped from earth
hook: You do not need stone to build a great capital.
story: The Chimú capital contained large walled compounds, workshops, and systems for managing water. Its layout made social and political divisions part of the city itself.
consequence: Urban design organised resources—and reflected who held power.
caution: This date is an approximate anchor near the kingdom’s high point. Archaeological layouts reveal structure more easily than the thoughts of ordinary residents.

title: Memory made monumental
hook: A memorial becomes a meeting of craft traditions.
story: Shah Jahan commissioned the Taj Mahal complex in memory of Mumtaz Mahal. Architects and craftspeople brought together design, calligraphy, stonework, gardens, and water.
consequence: A court’s resources enabled an enduring work of architecture.
caution: Different parts were completed at different times. The celebrated monument was a collective achievement, not the work of one pair of hands.

title: Two texts, different promises
hook: What happens when the same agreement does not say the same thing?
story: Māori rangatira and representatives of the British Crown signed Te Tiriti o Waitangi and the Treaty of Waitangi. Important differences between the Māori and English texts shaped later disagreement.
consequence: The agreement became central to continuing struggles over authority, land, and rights.
caution: Almost all rangatira signed the Māori text. Translating its promises simply as surrendering sovereignty obscures a central issue.

sources.title: NZ History · The Treaty in brief
NZ History · Differences between the texts

title: An island nation chooses its future
hook: The story of decolonisation reaches far beyond large continents.
story: Western Samoa became independent from New Zealand administration on 1 January 1962. Independence followed a long history of Samoan resistance and political organisation.
consequence: A Pacific nation regained control of its own government.
caution: The history concerns Western Samoa, now Samoa, and should not be confused with the different political history of American Samoa.

title: The land was never empty
hook: A community’s relationship with land challenges a legal fiction.
story: The High Court of Australia recognised the Meriam people’s native title in the Mabo decision. The case rejected the idea that Australia had belonged to no one before British colonisation.
consequence: Australian law recognised a basis for Indigenous native title.
caution: The decision did not automatically return all land or settle every claim. The map locates the community’s island, not the court.

sources.title: National Museum of Australia · Mabo decision
